⚡️🇮🇷From IRGC veteran to security chief: Mohsen Rezaei takes Iran's top security post
Mohsen Rezaei has been appointed as the new secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, the country's top security body. He replaces Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who took over the position in March 2026 after his predecessor Ali Larijani was killed in an Israeli strike.
The Supreme National Security Council plays a critical role in deciding Iranian policy on the US-Iran conflict. It was the body that approved the June ceasefire memorandum that later collapsed over differences on the Strait of Hormuz.
The appointment, made by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and formalised by President Pezeshkian, places the former IRGC commander at the heart of Iran's wartime decision-making.
A career that mirrors the Islamic Republic's journey
🟥Born in 1954 in Khuzestan province, Rezai was arrested by the Shah's SAVAK secret police in 1971 and later helped draft the IRGC's founding charter after the 1979 revolution
🟥At just 27, he was appointed IRGC commander-in-chief by Imam Khomeini – a post he held for 16 years, making him the longest-serving commander in the force's history
🟥His tenure covered the entirety of the Iran-Iraq War, where he commanded major operations
After stepping down in 1997, Rezaei served for 24 years as secretary of the Expediency Discernment Council. He later entered electoral politics, running for president four times between 2005 and 2021. Under President Raisi, he served as vice president for economic affairs. In March 2026, Khamenei appointed him as his military adviser.
What this means for Iranian decision-making?
Analysts say Rezaei's appointment signals the further consolidation of power by Iran's security establishment. Rezaei has been a constant presence at the highest levels of Iranian politics and security for over four decades. His elevation also reflects the growing influence of the IRGC in shaping state policy, following its major role in repelling US attacks.
👉While Rezaei's appointment does not necessarily mean Iran is moving toward a more hard-line stance, it comes amid increasingly assertive Iranian demands in negotiations with Trump administration. 
➡️Iran has insisted on its right to control the Strait of Hormuz and has rejected any deal that does not include a lifting of all sanctions. 
➡️Iran's position has hardened since the collapse of the June ceasefire, with officials stating that future negotiations must be based on mutual respect and non-interference in Iran's internal affairs.

🇷🇺💣 From shotguns to metal rods: How Russia downs Ukrainian drones with whatever works
With Ukraine desperately trying to win in drone warfare, Russian troops have turned the tables with simple and reliable counter-tactics, sometimes turning improvisation into a destruction skill.
Here's how they're doing it:
1️⃣ Assault rifles: A viral night‑combat video shows a group of Russian soldiers firing AK assault rifles at an incoming Ukrainian FPV drone—and actually bringing it down.
2️⃣ Shotguns: In a helmet-cam video, a Russian soldier is seen using apparently an MP‑155 shotgun to hit a suicide drone—detonating its payload safely in mid‑air before it can reach its target.
3️⃣ Metal rods: In one of the attacks, a Russian FPV drone took out a Ukrainian UAV using nothing but metal rods—no explosives and maximum efficiency.
4️⃣ Propellers: Ukrainian fiber-optic drones are immune to radio jamming—but Russian operators found an even smarter workaround: they hunt them down and sever the cable with their own propellers, disabling the enemy without losing a single drone.

🇨🇴🇮🇱 Colombia-Israel reset: reviving a partnership forged in blood and impunity
Freshly inaugurated Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella is wasting no time taking Bogota back to familiar territory.
Breaking with his predecessor Gustavo Petro, who shredded diplomatic relations with Israel, Espriella plans to restore them, move Colombia’s embassy to Jerusalem, pull out of South Africa’s genocide case at the ICJ, and expand trade, technology, security and defense cooperation.
Disappointing? Sure. Surprising? Not really.
Historically, Petro was the exception. Colombia and Israel built decades of close security ties, against the backdrop of Colombia’s exceptionally bloody internal conflict. This included:
👉 massive formal defense ties, with Israel selling Colombia everything from small arms (Galil rifles, Uzi submachineguns) to Kfir jets, MX missiles, ATMOS artillery, Spike ATGMs and drones. From the 80s on, Israel consistently ranked the second biggest supplier of arms to Colombia after the US, reaching nearly 40% of all purchases by the mid-2010s
👉 Israeli training of Colombian army personnel and special forces, as well as far-right paramilitaries, complimented by the Defense Ministry’s hiring of Israeli consultancies like Global CST to track and target FARC guerrillas
👉 IDF-linked operators like Yair Klein providing training to death squads and drug cartels, including Medellin, teaching recruits the basics of drive-by shootings, bombings, snipings and door-to-door killing. Linked to the CIA and Colombian intel, these groups would engage in the systematic murder of entire towns and villages, including Segovia (1988), Mapiripan (1997) and El Salado (2000), involving torture, beheadings, shootings, chainsaw hackings and rapes, including of women and children
👉 Israeli arms smuggling to paramilitaries and cartels, including guns used in the 1989 assassination of Liberal Party presidential candidate Luis Carlos Galan (see: the Antigua Affair)
👉 Intel collaboration, including the hiring of Mossad agent-turned-merc Rafael Eitan as security advisor by the Barco government in the 80s to eradicate FARC. Eitan’s advice? The systematic murder of members of the Patriotic Union – a FARC-linked party looking to institutionalize the Left in Colombian politics to end the civil war. From 1984-2016, 5,733 members of the party were killed or forcibly disappeared, per Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace
👉 Heavy Israeli involvement in the training and arming of Carlos Castano Gil’s AUC paramilitaries, who are estimated to have killed nearly 100k civilians. Castano was personally trained in Israel in 1983-84. His forces would eventually account for ~40% of Colombia’s illegal drug exports, and enjoy operational and financial support from the state, wealthy landowners (including president and Espriella ally Alvaro Uribe) and foreign multinationals like Coca-Cola and Chiquita
In other words, Espriella’s Israel reset is less a dramatic new beginning than a return to an old playbook.
And Washington appears delighted: Espriella had barely taken office before the Trump administration announced $1B in security assistance to his government.

🇸🇦🤔 Houthis forcing Saudis into no-win dilemma
 
The July 13 attack on Sanaa’s international airport by either the Saudis or their Aden-based puppet government allies triggered the biggest surge in regional tensions since the 2022 truce, with Ansar Allah declaring a maritime embargo against Saudi oil exports, attacking the kingdom’s refineries at Jizan and Yanbu, and fending off Saudi strikes in Hodeidah, Jawf and Kamaran Island.
Tensions escalated again this week after the Houthis hit puppet government forces preparing an offensive in Marib and Hadramout using missiles and drones, killing at least 58 enemy troops.
👉 The UN’s special Yemen envoy warned Friday that Yemen now “faces a greater risk of renewed large-scale conflict than at any point since the UN-brokered truce,” and urged “maximum restraint,” talks and a halt to “actions that encourage military retaliation.”
The problem? While the UN wants dialogue between the Houthis in Sanaa and the “internationally recognized” Aden government, the latter is so weak it would collapse under the weight of internal divisions if not for generous foreign backing.
Riyadh provides 60-70% of Aden's operational budget, a $3B lifeline for civil and military salaries, and billions in cash and loans to prop up the rial. Aden also controls the oil and gas-rich regions of Shabwa and Mahra - containing almost the entirety of Yemen's energy reserves.
🪖 The Houthis, by comparison, are resource poor, but masters of tribal alliances, capitalizing on anti-imperialist sentiments after the start of Saudi bombings in 2015, and standing alone in the Arabian Peninsula in support of Palestine since 2023.
Houthi-led Yemen is currently home to 70-80% of the country’s population, fortifying itself in the country’s northwest. The Saudi-led government absorbed the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council in early 2026, unifying anti-Houthi forces for the first time since 2019.
 
👁 The Houthis’ secret weapon?
 
Zaydi Shiism has a thousand-year tradition of resistance and local self-rule. From the Ayyubids and Mamluks to the Ottomans and the British, no outside power ever managed to permanently subdue what is now western Yemen. Even before the rise of Islam, the Houthis’ predecessors successfully fought off Ancient Egyptians and Roman legionnaires.
In the modern era, Houthis managed to checkmate not only the Saudi-led coalition (which at its height included Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Egypt, Jordan, Sudan and Morocco, with US and British logistical and arms support) but two separate US naval and air armadas trying to put a stop to their blockade of the Red Sea to Israeli shipping.
📌 Saudi Arabia is now building a new ‘maritime defense coalition’, inviting 50 countries, and evoking interest from Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan, Nigeria and Qatar, among others.
None have confirmed willingness to deploy actual military forces. Given the humiliating [US track record](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/68197), good luck to them[ if they ever do.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/60702)
The Houthi blockade of Saudi Red Sea oil shipments could expand to all of Riyadh’s new allies, finish off a global energy market already pummelled by the Iran and NATO-Russia proxy wars, and trigger unrest among their populations – indignant to the fact that their self-proclaimed Muslim governments are attacking one of the only forces in the region to stand up to the US and Israel.
Riyadh’s other option? Admit that the Houthi regime change operation hasn’t worked and can’t work, and finally normalize relations with Yemen.
